authoring: blind — authored from clone reads only, no retrieval run; every expect clause grep-verified (whitespace-normalized substring) in the named file; corpus is the section-split mirror (corpus-ecma262-sections)

ecma262.shape_risk: Half of the 2,341 section files are under 1 KB (median 1,016 B; largest 27 KB), so ranking cannot lean on length or code density — signal sits in a short emu-clause diluted by the shared template (breadcrumb first line plus <emu-clause>/<h1> header markup) repeated verbatim in every file. Hundreds of near-duplicate per-method sections (iterator .next variants, typed-array and prototype wrappers) reuse boilerplate like "a normal completion containing", so abstract-operation queries can tie dozens of files while the definitive step lives in one small file. Facts carried in <emu-note> blocks (527 files, versus 1,395 with <emu-alg> steps and 277 with <emu-grammar> tables) sit in trailing prose a chunker may drop, and inline spec markup (*+0*, |StringNumericLiteral|, _x_, <sub>) blocks naive term matching between a natural-language query and the verbatim text.

queries.expect: For each own property key _propertyKey_ of _obj_ such that _propertyKey_ is an array index, in ascending numeric index order, do

queries.expect: “!” is used to assert that a Completion Record is normal and unwrap it.

queries.q: which string forms are accepted when converting a string to a number — surrounding whitespace, leading zeros, Infinity — and how does that grammar differ from numeric literal syntax
queries.expect: A |StringNumericLiteral| that is empty or contains only white space is converted to *+0*<sub>𝔽</sub>

queries.q: when is a parser allowed to pretend a semicolon was present in the source, and which productions are restricted so that a newline forces one
queries.expect: a semicolon is never inserted automatically if the semicolon would then be parsed as an empty statement

queries.q: when two strings are compared with the less-than operator, is the comparison over code points or UTF-16 code units, and does Unicode normalization matter
